title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Why Causal Inference?
Sound causal reasoning is essential to pharmacometrics (Rogers, Maas, and Pitarch (2023)). A motivating premise of this book is that pharmacometricians will be better able to engage in causal reasoning with stochastic data if they are able to avail themselves of the formal vocabulary, notation, and concepts of formal causal inference. While this book may introduce the reader to some new analytic techniques, our emphasis will be on causal concepts as an aid to elicitation and interpretation, as suggested in the figure below.
Our perspective is that causal reasoning is especially important in pharmacometrics because it is often the case that pharmacometric questions must be addressed without the benefit of a dedicated randomized trial. As such, our goal is often not to provide the gold standard evidence that would result from a randomized trial, but rather to foster high-quality decision making when the ideal data is not available at the time the decision needs to be made, as suggested in the following figure.

title: 2  Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs
text:
2.1 What is a Causal DAG?
First, a distinction: the Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) discussed here will be specifically causal DAGs which, as the name suggests, convey causal information. In principle, DAGs can also be used to convey non-causal information (e.g. they are sometimes used to specify hierarchical models, which may or may not have causal interpretability), but in the context of this book, a “DAG” can always be understood to have causal semantics attached to it.
In the context of causal inference, DAGs consist of nodes, representing variables, and “directed edges” (a.k.a. arrows), representing causal dependencies between the variables. A proper DAG will contain only unidirectional arrows and will not contain directed loops (“acyclic”), corresponding to the notion that there can be no instantaneous causal feedback (feedback in general can be represented, but it must proceed in a temporal sequence).

title: 2  Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs
text:
2.2 DAG conventions in this book
Our graphical conventions in this book are intended to be similar to those used in the popular “dagitty” web application (Textor et al. (2016)), but with some modifications to better support readers who are red-green colorblind. The conventions we will use are:

The pathway(s) of causal dependence that we wish to quantify will be shown in blue (whereas in dagitty they show in green).
We won’t graphically distinguish between treatment nodes, outcome nodes, and other nodes. However, the previous convention makes it clear how to identify the treatment and outcome nodes, by determining where the blue arrows originate and terminate.
Biasing pathways (or unblocked “backdoor paths” to use the technical term that we will discuss later) will be shown in red.
Adjusted variables (variables that we control for in our analyses) will be depicted with rectangle-shaped nodes.
Causal dependencies that are neither biasing nor of direct interest will be depicted in gray (or “grey”, if you prefer).
Dashed lines to represent potential causal dependencies of a more speculative nature.

We illustrate these conventions in comparison to dagitty conventions in the following figures:

title: 2  Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs
text:
2.3 Competing terminology
Pharmacometrics and causal inference grew up in different communities, and several everyday words carry different meanings in each. The most important example is “exposure”: to a pharmacometrician, exposure is a drug concentration (or a summary of one, such as \(AUC\)), whereas in the causal inference literature, “exposure” is simply the name for the variable whose causal effect we want to estimate, whatever that variable happens to be. For example, when the question is how dose affects \(AUC\), the causal “exposure” is dose, and the pharmacometric exposure (\(AUC\)) is the outcome. Table 2.1 summarizes the terms most likely to cause confusion.



Table 2.1: Terms with different meanings in causal inference and pharmacometrics.










Term
In causal inference
In pharmacometrics




Exposure
The variable whose causal effect is of interest, often denoted \(A\). It may be a dose, a concentration, a drug, a behavior, etc. Synonymous with “treatment”
Drug concentration in the body \(C(t)\), or a summary of the concentration–time profile over a dosing interval (\(AUC\), \(C_{max}\), \(C_{trough}\))


Treatment or Intervention
Synonyms for exposure. It could correspond to a variable that is actually subject to manipulation, or to a merely hypothetical manipulation
Typically a variable like dose that is actually subject to manipulation


Time-varying exposure
An exposure whose value can change over follow-up, e.g. could be time-varying dose
The concentration–time profile, \(C(t)\).


Point exposure
An exposure that nominally occurs at a single point in time, as opposed to one that varies over follow-up.
Understood most naturally as a concentration at a specified time.






Where possible, we will use the word “exposure” in the causal inference sense, and we will say “drug concentration” or name the specific metric (e.g. \(AUC\)) when we mean pharmacokinetic exposure. One exception (sorry!): where we write “exposure-response”, you can assume that we are talking about the effect of pharmacokinetic exposure on response (in contrast to “dose-response”).

title: 2  Causal Directed Acyclic Graphs
text:
2.4 Examples of DAGs in Pharmacometrics

2.4.1 Dose-Response in an Individual Randomized Controlled Trial
From a causal perspective, the distinctive feature of a randomized controlled trial (RCT) is the the randomized intervention doesn’t have any causal antecedents, or parents. In the following figure representing a dose-randomized trial, this is represented graphically by the absence of any arrows going into dose \(D\). On the other hand, there may be many factors, some measured (represented below by \(L\)) and some unmeasured (represented below by \(U\)), that affect the response:








Figure 2.4: Randomized controlled trial with a precision covariate \(L\). There is no arrow from \(L\) to \(D\).





Because the trial was randomized, we know that neither \(L\) nor \(U\) is a cause of \(D\). Note that this important knowledge is conveyed in the graph by the absence of arrows into \(D\). This is a special case of a more general principle: depicted arrows merely indicate the plausibility of a causal relationship, while the most consequential assumptions are indicated by the arrows that are not there.
Strictly from a causal inference perspective, there would be no need to adjust for either \(L\) or \(U\) in analyzing data from this RCT. Because \(D\) and \(R\) cannot have any common causes in this RCT setting, there can be no confounding, and there is therefore no need – again, from a causal inference perspective – for adjustment. However, this is a limited perspective that doesn’t tell the whole story. The special preoccupation of causal inference is bias, and there is no opportunity for bias due to confounding in the above scenario. On the other hand precision never ceases to important (even if our DAG has nothing to say about it), and precision in statistical estimation can often be improved by adjusting for covariates such as \(L\), even when such adjustment is not needed to remove bias. In the RCT context, such covariates are sometimes referred to as precision covariates. The special power of RCTs is that they result in marginally unbiased estimates of treatment effects, even if there are many unknown factors like \(U\) that influence the response.


2.4.2 Exposure as a Mediator of Dose-Response
In pharmacometrics, a common causal structure links dose \(D\) to an exposure metric \(E\) (e.g. AUC or \(C_\text{max}\)) and then to a response \(R\). The following DAGs illustrate three important variants of this structure.
In the simplest case, the effect of \(D\) on \(R\) is fully mediated by \(E\). A mediator is a node on the pathway between intervention and outcome. Full mediation is a strong assumption.








Figure 2.5: Dose (\(D\)), exposure (\(E\)) and response (\(R\)), with the effect of dose fully mediated by exposure.





A direct path from \(D\) to \(R\) (bypassing \(E\)) can be added to capture effects not mediated through the measured exposure. The total causal effect of \(D\) on \(R\) then decomposes as: \[\text{Total effect} = \text{Direct effect } (D \to R) + \text{Indirect effect } (D \to E \to R).\] This distinction matters in practice: when the measured exposure (e.g. plasma AUC) is a poor proxy for exposure at the site of action — such as the brain or lungs — the D-to-E-to-R path alone may not capture the full effect of dose on response. In such settings, estimating the total effect of \(D\) on \(R\) directly is a more robust target.








Figure 2.6: D-E-R DAG with a direct effect of dose on response that bypasses the measured exposure.







2.4.3 Exposure-Response
In some cases, e.g. for many systemically acting small molecules, there may be good reason to believe that systemic exposure fully mediates the effect of dose on response. When this is in fact the case, it will often be of interest to characterize the effect of exposure on response because, as summarized by Braniff (2026)

While dose is a natural intervention variable, dose–response inference is specific to the formulation, regimen, and delivery mechanism studied and does not generalize readily across many design dimensions relevant to development. A key contribution of ER analysis is the decomposition of the dose-exposure-response relation into two separable questions: is the dose achieving adequate exposure, and is that exposure sufficient to drive response? This decomposition enables modular optimization so that formulation, regimen, and delivery can be modified while maintaining clear exposure targets, guiding development across changing phases and populations.

As appealing as this decomposition is, it can only be achieved under specific conditions. We already discussed on of these conditions above: the argument only works when the effect of dose on response is fully mediated through the exposure metric. We now consider an additional requirement.
When a covariate \(L\) affects both \(E\) and \(R\), it confounds the exposure-response relationship, opening a biasing backdoor path \(E \leftarrow L \rightarrow R\). A concrete example: in an obesity indication, body weight (\(L\)) influences drug exposure (\(E\)) through its effect on pharmacokinetics, while also independently increasing the risk of cardiovascular events (\(R\)). A naïve exposure-response analysis would therefore conflate the drug effect with the background cardiovascular risk driven by body weight.








Figure 2.7: E-R DAG in which a covariate \(L\) (e.g. body weight) confounds the exposure-response relationship. Note that the blue arrows now begin at \(E\), indicating that exposure is now our treatment variable of interest.













Figure 2.8: Adjustment for bodyweight closes the backdoor path.
















































































































































































































































































































































Braniff, N. 2026. “Causal Exposure Response Analysis: Estimands, Time-Varying Confounding, and the Parametric g-Formula.”


Textor, Johannes, Benito van der Zander, Mark S Gilthorpe, Maciej Liskiewicz, and George Th Ellison. 2016. “Robust Causal Inference Using Directed Acyclic Graphs: The R Package ’Dagitty’.” Int. J. Epidemiol. 45 (6): 1887–94.

title: 3  Estimands
text:
3.1 Estimand Concepts from ICH E9 (R1)
The ICH E9(R1) addendum (ICH 2019) introduced a framework for stating precisely what a clinical trial is meant to estimate, before deciding how to estimate it. Its central idea is that a trial objective should be translated into an estimand: a precise description of the treatment effect of interest. Only then should one choose an estimator (the analysis method) and report the resulting estimate. Sensitivity analyses then probe how much the estimate depends on the assumptions of the estimator.
An estimand is defined by five attributes:
The fourth attribute is the main novelty of the addendum. ICH E9(R1) describes five strategies for handling intercurrent events:
Although the addendum does not use the formal language of causal inference, each of these attributes has a direct counterpart in potential outcome notation. In the remainder of this chapter, we use that notation to express estimands mathematically, and we return to the treatment policy and hypothetical strategies in the context of dose-exposure-response.

title: 3  Estimands
text:
Treatment: the treatment condition of interest and, where relevant, the alternative it is compared with.
Population: the patients targeted by the clinical question.
Variable (endpoint): the quantity measured on each patient to address the question.
Intercurrent events: how events occurring after treatment initiation that affect the interpretation or existence of the endpoint (e.g. treatment discontinuation, dose reduction, rescue medication, death) are accounted for.
Population-level summary: the summary measure used to compare treatment conditions (e.g. a difference in means, a risk ratio, a hazard ratio).



Treatment policy: the intercurrent event is considered part of the treatment strategy, and the endpoint is used regardless of whether it occurs.
Hypothetical: the effect is defined under a hypothetical scenario in which the intercurrent event would not occur (e.g. had no patients needed a dose reduction).
Composite variable: the occurrence of the intercurrent event is incorporated into the endpoint itself (e.g. counting discontinuation as treatment failure).
While on treatment: the endpoint is considered only up to the occurrence of the intercurrent event.
Principal stratum: the target population is restricted to the subpopulation in which the intercurrent event would (or would not) occur, under one or both treatments.

title: 3  Estimands
section: 3.2 Potential Outcomes and the Mathematical Representation of Estimands
text:
3.2 Potential Outcomes and the Mathematical Representation of Estimands
In order to express estimands mathematically, we need a notational system that distinguishes between what will happen if we let nature take its course, and what would happen if we were to intervene. For the second set of concepts, we will use potential outcome notation. The following exploration in R, adapted from the supplemental material of Rogers, Maas, and Pitarch (2023), is intended to develop intuitions about the differences between conditional distributions of observable quantities on the one hand, and potential outcome distributions on the other.
The fundamental problem of causal inference is that, when it comes to intervening on a single subject or experimental unit, we can only try one thing at a time. This constraint is summarized poetically in the words that Plato attributes to Heraclitus: “… all things move and nothing remains still … you cannot step twice into the same stream.” We can of course return to the same subject, or the same experimental unit, to evaluate a different intervention, but the experimental conditions will never quite be the same. For this reason, the potential outcome distributions associated with any real-world process will only ever be partially observable. In the R-based exploration that follows, we are able to free ourselves from this constraint by working with simulated data. In simulation world, we know all the “what-ifs” that we can’t directly observe in the real world.
For simplicity at the outset, we will consider a scenario with just two levels of treatment, referred to as “control” and “active” and indexed by 0 and 1, and two possible outcomes, corresponding to failure and success, also denoted with 0 and 1. We will simulate 4000 subjects. This number is sufficiently large to make the statistical imprecision in our estimates small in comparison to the treatment effect, so that – for didactic purposes – we can mostly ignore the usual distinction between population and sample, and we can focus exclusively on issues of bias. For each simulated subject, we will set the value of the potential outcome \(Y^0\) (represented in our simulated dataset as Y0 ), corresponding to the outcome that would occur if the given subject receives the control treatment, and the potential outcome \(Y^1\) (represented in our simulated dataset as Y1), corresponding to the outcome that would occur if the given subject receives the active treatment.

set.seed(1)
potential_outcomes <- tibble(
SUBJID = 1:4000,
Y0 = c(rep(1, 1000), rep(0, 1000), rep(1, 500), rep(0, 1500)),
Y1 = c(rep(1, 1000), rep(0, 1000), rep(0, 500), rep(1, 1500))
)
potential_outcomes %>%
group_by(Y0, Y1) %>%
summarise(NSUBJ = n(), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 4 × 3
     Y0    Y1 NSUBJ
  <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1     0     0  1000
2     0     1  1500
3     1     0   500
4     1     1  1000



potential_outcomes <- potential_outcomes %>%
  mutate(p_ecog_1 = case_when(Y0 + Y1 == 0 ~ 0.75,
                              Y0 + Y1 == 1 ~ 0.5,
                              Y0 + Y1 == 2 ~ 0.25),
         ECOG = rbinom(n(), 1, p_ecog_1),
         NEUTROPHILS = exp(rnorm(n(), 0, 0.5))
         ) %>%
  select(-p_ecog_1)


obs_study <- potential_outcomes %>%
  mutate(
    p_novel = case_when(ECOG == 0 ~ 0.2,
                        ECOG == 1 ~ 0.8),
    A_NAT = rbinom(n(), 1, p_novel),
    TRT = A_NAT,
    YOBS = if_else(TRT == 0, Y0, Y1)
  ) %>%
  select(-p_novel)
obs_study %>% slice_sample(n=10)

# A tibble: 10 × 8
   SUBJID    Y0    Y1  ECOG NEUTROPHILS A_NAT   TRT  YOBS
    <int> <dbl> <dbl> <int>       <dbl> <int> <int> <dbl>
 1   2720     0     1     0       1.23      0     0     0
 2   2398     1     0     0       0.494     0     0     1
 3   1044     0     0     1       0.491     1     1     0
 4   1351     0     0     1       1.37      1     1     0
 5    618     1     1     0       0.551     0     0     1
 6    451     1     1     1       0.627     1     1     1
 7   1076     0     0     1       1.06      1     1     0
 8   3882     0     1     0       0.554     0     0     0
 9    301     1     1     0       0.856     0     0     1
10   3232     0     1     0       1.25      0     0     0


Now that we have a treatment variable and an observed outcome variable, we can investigate the differences between conditional distributions of observed values and potential outcome distributions. This expected value \(E[Y(A=0)]\), a.k.a. \(P(Y(A=0)=1)\) corresponds to this quantity in our code:

obs_study %>% pull(Y0) %>% mean()

[1] 0.375


Contrast that with the expected value \(E[Y | A = 0]\), a.k.a. \(P(Y = 1 | A = 0)\):

obs_study %>% filter(A_NAT == 0) %>% pull(YOBS) %>% mean()

[1] 0.4517413


Comparing the last two quantities tips us off to the following inequality:
\[ E[Y(A=0)] \neq E[Y | A=0] \]
This difference in our unadjusted summaries generally also show up when we look at comparative statistics, such as mean treatment differences. The true (causal) average treatment effect, the “ATE” can be expressed mathematically as
\[ E[ Y(A=1) - Y(A=0) ]. \] The corresponding operation in our code is:

obs_study %>% 
  mutate(ITE = Y1 - Y0) %>% 
  summarise(ATE = mean(ITE)) 

# A tibble: 1 × 1
    ATE
  <dbl>
1  0.25


Compare that to the difference in the observed treatment means. The expected value for this latter quantity can be expressed as:
\[ E[Y | A= 1] - E[Y | A = 0] \]

obs_study %>% 
  group_by(A_NAT) %>% 
  summarise(Ybar = mean(YOBS), .groups = "drop") %>% 
  summarise(UnadjustedEstimateTE = diff(Ybar))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  UnadjustedEstimateTE
                 <dbl>
1               0.0990


We can see that in this case, a naïve analysis would result in a substantial underestimate of the treatment effect. This is because the expected value of our estimate is not equal to the causal quantity of interest:
\[  E[ Y(A=1) - Y(A=0) ] \neq E[Y | A= 1] - E[Y | A = 0] \]
We can also consider several conditional average treatment effects or “CATEs”. For example, the CATEs conditional on baseline ECOG can be expressed mathematically as:
\[ E[ Y(A=1) - Y(A=0) \,|\, \mathit{ECOG}=0] \,\, \mbox{ and } \,\,E[ Y(A=1) - Y(A=0) \,|\, \mathit{ECOG}=1] \] \[ E[ Y(\mathit{Dose}=1) - Y(\mathit{Dose=0}) \,|\, \mathit{ECOG}=0] \,\, \mbox{ and } \,\,E[ Y(A=1) - Y(A=0) \,|\, \mathit{ECOG}=1] \]

obs_study %>% 
  mutate(ITE = Y1 - Y0) %>% 
  group_by(ECOG) %>% 
  summarise(CATE = mean(ITE))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
   ECOG  CATE
  <int> <dbl>
1     0 0.248
2     1 0.252


We can see that these are actually well-approximated by the corresponding conditional distributions in the observable data:

obs_study %>% 
  group_by(A_NAT, ECOG) %>% 
  summarise(Ybar = mean(YOBS), .groups = "drop") %>% 
  group_by(ECOG) %>% 
  summarise(ConditionalEstimateTE = diff(Ybar))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
   ECOG ConditionalEstimateTE
  <int>                 <dbl>
1     0                 0.263
2     1                 0.242


A number of the other variants of causal effects are simply special cases of conditional average treatment effects. For example, the average treatment effect in the treated (“ATT”) is simply the CATE that results from conditioning on being treated.

title: 3  Estimands
text:
3.3 Dose-exposure-response Estimands
A typical development program proceeds by selecting doses primarily based on Phase 2 data, and then confirming the efficacy and safety at the given dose(s) in Phase 3. Whereas hypothetical questions may appropriately play a greater role in earlier stages of development, the late development context gives increasing consideration to directly pragmatic questions about use, “in the wild”. (For example, in early development, the question, “What would have been the efficacy if adherence to the prescribed dosing regimen had been better?” will be relevant if it is possible to achieve better adherence with, e.g., changes in formulation or route of administration or dosing frequency; such hypotheticals become less relevant in later development when the goal confirm that a particular posology achieves acceptable benefit risk. Bartels et al. (2025) examines a hypothetical estimand of this nature.) Late development is therefore a context where treatment policy estimands have special relevance Fleming et al. (2025). Several examples of such estimands for the purpose of dose selection and dose justification in the late development context were considered in Bartels et al. (2026).
The presumed causal structure in Bartels et al. (2026) is summarized in the following DAG. Note that we appear to have broken our own rules, since the graph includes undirected edges (with no arrowheads) between the covariate (“L”) variables. This is just our way of signaling that the variables represented in these three nodes have a joint distribution with a statistical dependence structure that we acknowledge without bothering to explain the causal dependencies that give rise to the statistical dependencies (it turns out that we don’t need to specify that level of detail for the relevant derivations to work).








Figure 3.1: Presumed causal structure for dose, early exposure, dose reduction and platelets in Bartels et al. (2026). Undirected gray edges link covariates that are statistically dependent.





We now review these scenarios.

3.3.1 Scenario 1: No difference between treatment policy and hypothetical estimands
In the first scenario, we treat dose reduction itself as the endpoint of interest (the idea being that, in this context, a dose reduction signifies a starting dose that was too high), and we proceed as if there are no intercurrent events between the initial dose assignment and dose reductions. Given that assumption, there is no distinction between the treatment policy estimand and the hypothetical estimand (because we can’t even entertain intervening on the intercurrent events if there are no intercurrent events!)








Figure 3.2: Scenario 1: dose reduction (\(R\)) is the endpoint.





The DAG expresses our assumptions, and our estimand may be expressed as:
\[ E\left[R(D=d) \,\,| \,\, \mathit{ATLL}\right] \] For now we defer the question of how best to estimate this quantity. We will come to that in later chapters in our discussion of adjustment methods such as \(g\)-estimation.


3.3.2 Scenario 2: Forced to choose treatment policy or hypothetical estimand
We now consider a different endpoint, taking platelets at study end as the primary endpoint of interest. In this framing, dose reduction must be considered as an intercurrent event, because such events may occur at times after dose assignment and before measurement of the outcome. We assume the same causal connections as above:








Figure 3.3: Scenario 2: platelets at study end (\(Y\)) are the endpoint, and dose reduction is an intercurrent event.





Our treatment policy estimand has the same form as in the previous scenario, but with \(Y\) rather than \(R\) as our outcome:
\[ E\left[Y(D=d) \,\,| \,\, \mathit{ATLL}\right] \]
If our interest were in the hypothetical scenario where dose reductions do not occur, there would be no easy way to represent this on the DAG; instead, a more complex graphical representation, known as a single-world intervention graph (SWIG) could be used. For the time being, we maintain on our focus on the treatment policy estimand, and we can defer the introduction of SWIG notation. We can, however, represent hypothetical estimands mathematically, but expanding our potential outcome notation to signal two interventions: the primary intervention on dose and a hypothetical intervention in which we prevent dose reductions:
\[ E\left[Y(D=d, R=0) \,\,| \,\, \mathit{ATLL}\right] \]


3.3.3 Scenario 3: Special Target Population
In the third scenario, we maintain a focus on platelets as our outcome of interest, but with an eye toward labeling recommendations for special populations, we adjust our target population to be the renally impaired (as an operational definition, we will define this as the subset of the overall ATLL population with creatinine clearance < 60 mL/min). Here our DAG would remain as above, but we now take our estimands to be:
\[ E[Y(D=d) \,\,| ATLL, CRCL < 60] \]

Pharmacol. 14 (1): 68–81.


Bartels, Christian, Yuchen Wang, Jonathan French, and James Rogers. 2026. “Some Common Dose-Exposure-Response Estimands and Conditions for Their Causal Identifiability.” CPT Pharmacometrics Syst. Pharmacol. 15 (2): e70202.

title: 4  G-formula and G-computation
text:
4.0.1 What this chapter is about
In this chapter we cover g-formula1, which is a prediction-based approach to deriving valid causal inferences. G-formula is not the only way to derive valid causal inferences – for example, in subsequent chapters we will see alternative methods based on inverse propensity weighting – but g-formula is especially well suited to pharmacometric analyses that already involve modeling and simulation.

title: 4  G-formula and G-computation
section: 4.1 G-formula for point exposures with baseline confounding
text:
4.1 G-formula for point exposures with baseline confounding
When we are interested in the effects of a point exposure on a response, we will specifically be concerned with baseline confounding (time-varying confounding can’t arise if the exposure variable is not itself time-varying). Baseline confounding has a very intuitive remedy, which is sometimes referred to as “standardization”. Standardization is a special case of g-formula.

4.1.1 Example: dose and AUC in a single ascending dose study
Consider a first-in-human single ascending dose (SAD) study with 5 cohorts. Let’s suppose that the clinical development plan is aiming to develop the drug in a target population that is 50% men and 50% women. Suppose that, to address fetal safety concerns, the first four dose levels are tested in escalation cohorts that enroll men only. The highest dose is then studied in an expansion cohort that enrolls 50% men and 50% women. There may be good ethical reasons for such a design, but it confounds the relationship between dose and exposure.
In this case, the “point exposure” is \(\text{Dose}\), and \(AUC\) is the outcome. Let’s suppose we want to know how \(AUC\) changes as a function of dose in a target population composed of 50% men and 50% women.
To keep the example transparent, the PK is linear, and body weight is the only PK covariate. It acts on clearance through allometric scaling:
\[
CL_i = CL_{pop} \left(\frac{WT_i}{70}\right)^{0.75} e^{\eta_i},
\qquad AUC_i = \frac{\text{Dose}_i}{CL_i}
\]
By construction, sex affects \(AUC\) only through body size. Sex also determines which doses a subject can receive, because women only enter the study only in the expansion cohort. The DAG is shown below, with \(A\) = dose, \(Y\) = \(AUC\), \(S\) = sex, and \(W\) = body weight.








Figure 4.1: DAG for the SAD study. Sex (\(S\)) determines which doses (\(A\)) a subject can receive and, through body weight (\(W\)), affects AUC (\(Y\)).





In the absence of any adjustments for weight, the backdoor path \(A \leftarrow S \rightarrow W \rightarrow Y\) (red) is open, indicating that the (unadjusted) association between \(\text{Dose}\) and \(AUC\) is biased relative to the true causal effect. A naive comparison of \(AUC\) across doses therefore compares different populations as well as different doses. Either \(S\) or \(W\) blocks the path. We adjust for \(W\) (drawn as a rectangle) for a reason we explain below.

4.1.1.1 Simulating the study
The simulation below uses doses of 10, 30, 100 and 300 mg, with six men in each escalation cohort and 40 subjects (20 men, 20 women) in the expansion cohort at 300 mg. Body weight is log-normal, with a median of 85 kg in men and 65 kg in women.

sad_param <- list(
  doses   = c(10, 30, 100, 300),     # mg
  n_esc   = 6,                       # men per escalation cohort
  n_exp   = 40,                      # expansion cohort, 50% women
  exp_dose = 300,                    # expansion cohort dose (mg)
  wt_med  = c(Male = 85, Female = 65),  # kg
  wt_lsd  = 0.15,
  cl_pop  = 5,                       # L/h for a 70 kg subject
  cl_exp  = 0.75,                    # allometric exponent
  omega   = 0.25                     # SD of eta on CL
)

# Draw body weight, clearance and AUC for a set of subjects with given sex and dose
sad_pk <- function(dat, p = sad_param) {
  dat |>
    mutate(
      WT  = exp(rnorm(n(), log(p$wt_med[SEX]), p$wt_lsd)),
      CL  = p$cl_pop * (WT / 70)^p$cl_exp * exp(rnorm(n(), 0, p$omega)),
      AUC = DOSE / CL
    )
}

sad_simulate_trial <- function(p = sad_param) {
  escalation <- tibble(
    COHORT = "Escalation",
    DOSE   = rep(p$doses, each = p$n_esc),
    SEX    = "Male"
  )
  expansion <- tibble(
    COHORT = "Expansion",
    DOSE   = p$exp_dose,
    SEX    = rep(c("Male", "Female"), each = p$n_exp / 2)
  )
  bind_rows(escalation, expansion) |>
    mutate(ID = row_number(), .before = 1) |>
    sad_pk(p)
}

set.seed(20261109)
sad_dat <- sad_simulate_trial()

The figure shows dose-normalized \(AUC\) for each subject. If the PK is linear, \(AUC/\text{Dose}\) does not depend on dose, so any trend in this plot is not caused by dose. Women (who are only present at 300 mg) sit higher.

sad_dat |>
  mutate(SEX = factor(SEX, levels = c("Male", "Female"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(DOSE), AUC / DOSE, colour = SEX)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.5,
                                             seed = 1),
             size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Male = "#2a78d6", Female = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Dose (mg)", y = "AUC / Dose (h/L)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "top")







Figure 4.2: Dose-normalized AUC by dose and sex in the simulated SAD study. Women are enrolled only at the 300 mg dose.







4.1.1.2 Estimand and ground truth
Let \(Y(a)\) be the potential \(AUC\) for a subject if they received dose \(a\). Our target is the mean potential \(AUC\) at each dose in a 50/50 population of men and women. This is the population the drug will be used in.
\[ E[Y(a)], \quad a \in \{10, 30, 100, 300\} \]
Since we wrote the data-generating process, we can compute the truth by simulation: give every member of a large 50/50 population each dose in turn and average the resulting \(AUC\)s. This is the “correct simulation logic” that we referred to at the outset of the chapter. In the simulation, dose is set by intervention on every person, not by the cohort someone happened to be enrolled in.

set.seed(1)
sad_truth <- tibble(SEX = rep(c("Male", "Female"), each = 5e5)) |>
  cross_join(tibble(DOSE = sad_param$doses)) |>
  sad_pk() |>
  group_by(DOSE) |>
  summarise(Truth = mean(AUC))

Note that sad_pk() draws a new weight and \(\eta\) for each subject–dose row. That is harmless here because the truth is a population mean, not an individual-level contrast.


4.1.1.3 Naive analysis
The naive estimate of \(E[Y(a)]\) is the observed mean \(AUC\) among subjects who got dose \(a\):
\[ \hat{E}[Y \mid A = a] \]
This is the right answer only if the subjects at each dose are exchangeable with the target population. Here they are not: the escalation doses include men only.

sad_naive <- sad_dat |>
  group_by(DOSE) |>
  summarise(Naive = mean(AUC))



4.1.1.4 Standardization (the g-formula for a point exposure)
Because \(W\) blocks the backdoor path, conditional exchangeability holds given \(W\), and the g-formula for a point exposure is
\[
E[Y(a)] = \int E[Y \mid A = a, W = w] \, dF_W(w),
\]
where \(F_W\) is the distribution of body weight in the target population. There are two ingredients:

An outcome model for \(E[Y \mid A, W]\). We use a log-linear regression, which matches the structure of the PK model: \(\log AUC = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log \text{Dose} + \beta_2 \log WT + \varepsilon\).
A sample from \(F_W\). The expansion cohort is a 50/50 sample of the target population, so its observed weights can stand in for \(F_W\).

The task of integration can then be accomplished by averaging over the simulated values. For each dose \(a\), set every target subject’s dose to \(a\), predict their mean \(AUC\) from the model, and average:

sad_fit <- lm(log(AUC) ~ log(DOSE) + log(WT), data = sad_dat)

sad_target <- sad_dat |>
  filter(COHORT == "Expansion") |>
  select(ID, SEX, WT)

sad_std <- sad_target |>
  cross_join(tibble(DOSE = sad_param$doses)) |>
  mutate(
    # back-transform: the mean of a log-normal is exp(mu + sigma^2 / 2)
    PRED = exp(predict(sad_fit, newdata = pick(everything())) + sigma(sad_fit)^2 / 2)
  ) |>
  group_by(DOSE) |>
  summarise(Standardized = mean(PRED))

Note the subjects are fixed and only the dose changes across rows. Each target subject therefore appears once at every dose level. This is the counterfactual intervention “give everyone dose \(a\)” applied to the model. To develop an intution for what the cross-join is accomplishing in the code above, take a look at Kat Hoffman’s excellent Visual Guide to G-computation


4.1.1.5 Comparing the estimates

sad_naive |>
  left_join(sad_std, by = "DOSE") |>
  left_join(sad_truth, by = "DOSE") |>
  mutate(across(c(Naive, Standardized), list(bias = ~ 100 * (.x / Truth - 1)),
                .names = "{.col} bias (%)")) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, col.names = c("Dose (mg)", "Naive", "Standardized",
                                         "Truth", "Naive bias (%)",
                                         "Standardized bias (%)"))

That’s what I would have done in any case, even if I had never heard of standardization or g-formula!” If so, great, but don’t get too high on your horse yet: it will get more complicated when we get to time-varying confounding.

title: 4  G-formula and G-computation
section: 4.2 G-formula for time-varying exposure with longitudinal confounding
text:
4.2 G-formula for time-varying exposure with longitudinal confounding

4.2.1 Example illustrating plug-in G-formula
In the preceding example, the key confounding variable, weight, was continuously valued. Similarly, in many the applications in this book, both the confounding variable(s) and the exposure variable(s) will be continuous, and we will model their effects (as we did in the preceding example), using parametric regression. When we implement g-formula using parametric regression models, we are using parametric g-formula, and that variant of g-formula will be our primary focus in this book.
For didactic purposes however, it will be helpful to strip away the distraction of regression models as we begin our exploration of time-varying confounding. To do this, the following example implements the plug-in g-formula, which is a version of g-formula that can be computed using only the observed conditional means. The plug-in g-formula can only be used when all confounding variables and intervention variables are categorically valued. The following example is constructed to conform (somewhat artificially) to this requirement. The data are adapted from Table 21.1 in Hernán and Robins (2024).
In Hernán and Robins (2024) , the data are presented in the form of a summary table. The essential structure of that table is preserved below, albeit using variable names that correspond more closely to a standard pharmacometric problem in oncology2. The original example is described as arising from a sequentially. Note that we have preserved the exorbitant sample sizes of the original example because we want to focus on issues of bias in estimation (without the distraction of precision issues, which become relevant at lower sample sizes.)

summ_dat <- tibble(
  DOSE = rep(1, 8),
  AUC1 = rep(c("high", "low"), each = 4), 
  LOWNEUT = rep(rep(0:1, each = 2), 2), 
  AUC2 = rep(c("high", "low"), 4),
  N = 100 * c(24, 16, 24, 96, 48, 32, 16, 64), 
  ORR = 0.01 * rep(c(84, 52, 76, 44), each = 2)
)

In order to more easily analyze this data, we expand the summary table to one subject per row:

set.seed(2026)
subj_dat <- summ_dat |>
  mutate(N_RESP = round(N * ORR)) |>
  slice(rep(row_number(), N)) |>
  group_by(AUC1, LOWNEUT, AUC2) |>
  mutate(RESP = as.integer(row_number() <= N_RESP)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  slice_sample(prop = 1) |>
  mutate(ID = row_number()) |>
  select(ID, DOSE, AUC1, LOWNEUT, AUC2, RESP)

The subject-level data subj_dat describe a two-period study. Map the variables to the usual notation as follows:



Table 4.2: Variables in the two-period example and their notation.










Symbol
Variable
Meaning




\(D_1\)
DOSE1
Dose for period 1 (high for everyone)


\(A_1\)
AUC1
Area under \(C(t)\) curve in period 1 (high or low)


\(L_2\)
LOWNEUT
Low neutrophil count after period 1 (0/1)


\(D_2\)
DOSE2
Dose period 2 (high or low)


\(A_2\)
AUC2
Area under \(C(t)\) curve in period 2 (high or low)


\(Y\)
RESP
Objective response (0/1)






Though it’s not obvious (yet) these data have been constructed so that exposure has no effect on response. However, we will willfully forget this fact when it comes time to draw the DAG, because in practice we would never know the true data generating mechanism. The DAG below, adapted from Figure 20.3 of Hernán and Robins (2024), shows the assumed causal structure. \(U\) is an unmeasured common cause of \(L_2\) and \(Y\) (for example, underlying disease severity).
For purposes of this example, we will focus on how to estimate the causal effect of \(AUC\) on reponse (the “exposure-response” in the usual pharmacometric sense). Depending on the context, it might be sufficient to ignore \(AUC\) entirely and directly estimate the “dose-response” relationship instead. However, as summarized by Braniff (2026),

While dose is a natural intervention variable, dose–response inference is specific to the formulation, regimen, and delivery mechanism studied and does not generalize readily across many design dimensions relevant to development. A key contribution of ER analysis is the decomposition of the dose-exposure-response relation into two separable questions: is the dose achieving adequate exposure, and is that exposure sufficient to drive response? This decomposition enables modular optimization so that formulation, regimen, and delivery can be modified while maintaining clear exposure targets, guiding development across changing phases and populations.

When we adopt this perspective (as pharmacometricians most often do), we are implicitly treating \(AUC\) as the treatment or intervention variable. Even though we cannot directly intervene on \(AUC\), an exposure-response analysis is implicitly asking: “If we could intervene directly to change \(AUC\), what would happen to the response?”. Moreover specifically, we will adopt the perspective that we want to know the causal effect of an entire exposure trajectory, so the hypothetical intervention involves setting the value of both \(AUC1\) and \(AUC2\).








Figure 4.3: Assumed causal structure for the two-period example, adapted from Figure 20.3 of Hernán and Robins (2024). \(U\) is an unmeasured common cause of \(L_2\) and \(Y\).





In this simplified representation, \(L_2\) does not appear to be a time-varying covariate. Of course, we could easily add baseline neutrophiles as \(L_1\), but that would just a cosmetic change. The essential feature of the DAG that introduces time-varying confounding is the fact that \(L_2\), being downstream of \(A_1\) and upstream of \(A_2\), plays two roles:

It is a confounder of \(A_2\). Low neutrophils prompt a change in the period-2 dose (\(L_2 \rightarrow D_2\)), which in turn changes period-2 exposure (\(D_2 \rightarrow A_2\)). The backdoor path \(A_2 \leftarrow D_2 \leftarrow L_2 \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y\) (red) is open unless we condition on \(L_2\).
It is a collider on the path \(A_1 \rightarrow L_2 \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y\). This path is closed as long as we do not condition on \(L_2\) or on its descendant \(D_2\).

Because \(A_1\) affects \(L_2\), which in turn affects \(A_2\), this structure is called treatment–confounder feedback. Adjusting for \(L_2\) is needed to handle the first path but opens the second, so no single conditional analysis (adjusting or not adjusting for \(L_2\)) gives an unbiased estimate of the joint effect of \(A_1\) and \(A_2\).
There are several different exposure histories that we could theoretically compare:

“always high” \((a_1, a_2) = (\text{high}, \text{high})\),
“high-then-low” \((a_1, a_2) = (\text{high}, \text{low})\)
“always low” \((a_1, a_2) = (\text{low}, \text{low})\)

“low-then-high” \((a_1, a_2) = (\text{low}, \text{high})\).

Note that to compare any of the strategies listed above is to target a hypothetical estimand, as opposed to a treatment policy estimand. In a treatment policy perspective, the dose reduction would be considered as an intercurrent event, and would necessarily be incorporated into the treatment definition. By contrast, if we want to isolate the causal effect of exposure per se, we have to contrast hypothetical scenarios in which the intercurrent event has no effect. To simplify our discussion, we will compare the “always high” and “always low” strategies, but the following discussion would apply equally to a comparison of any of the hypothetical strategies.
We have yet to say exactly what g-formula is in general … please be patient, we will get there … but in this special two-timepoint case, the g-formula can be expressed as:
\[ E[Y(a_1, a_2)] = \sum_{l} E[Y \mid A_1 = a_1, L_2 = l, A_2 = a_2] \, \Pr(L_2 = l \mid A_1 = a_1) \]
In words: within each level of \(L_2\), take the mean response among subjects who actually followed the strategy, and then average over \(L_2\) using the distribution that \(L_2\) would have under \(a_1\). Note that the weights are \(\Pr(L_2 = l \mid A_1 = a_1)\), not the marginal \(\Pr(L_2 = l)\). This is what lets the g-formula handle a confounder that is itself affected by earlier exposure.
Plug-in g-computation means estimating each piece of the formula from the data and plugging the estimates in. Here every variable is discrete, so each piece is simply a sample proportion or mean.

4.2.1.1 Step 1: Distribution of \(L_2\) given \(A_1\)
Estimate \(\Pr(L_2 = l \mid A_1 = a_1)\) by the proportion of subjects in each level of LOWNEUT within each level of AUC1:

p_L <- subj_dat |>
  count(AUC1, LOWNEUT) |>
  group_by(AUC1) |>
  mutate(P_L = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()
p_L

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  AUC1  LOWNEUT     n   P_L
  <chr>   <int> <int> <dbl>
1 high        0  4000  0.25
2 high        1 12000  0.75
3 low         0  8000  0.5 
4 low         1  8000  0.5 


High period-1 exposure makes low neutrophils more likely (0.75 vs 0.5).


4.2.1.2 Step 2: Mean response given exposure history and \(L_2\)
Estimate \(E[Y \mid A_1 = a_1, L_2 = l, A_2 = a_2]\) by the observed response rate in each combination of AUC1, LOWNEUT and AUC2:

m_Y <- subj_dat |>
  group_by(AUC1, LOWNEUT, AUC2) |>
  summarise(n = n(), n_resp = sum(RESP), E_Y = mean(RESP), .groups = "drop")
m_Y

# A tibble: 8 × 6
  AUC1  LOWNEUT AUC2      n n_resp   E_Y
  <chr>   <int> <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl>
1 high        0 high   2400   2016  0.84
2 high        0 low    1600   1344  0.84
3 high        1 high   2400   1248  0.52
4 high        1 low    9600   4992  0.52
5 low         0 high   4800   3648  0.76
6 low         0 low    3200   2432  0.76
7 low         1 high   1600    704  0.44
8 low         1 low    6400   2816  0.44




4.2.1.3 Step 3: Combine for one strategy
For the “always high” strategy, keep the rows of m_Y with AUC1 == "high" and AUC2 == "high". Then attach the matching weights from Step 1 and form the weighted sum:

g_high <- m_Y |>
  filter(AUC1 == "high", AUC2 == "high") |>
  left_join(p_L |> select(AUC1, LOWNEUT, P_L), by = c("AUC1", "LOWNEUT")) |>
  mutate(CONTRIB = E_Y * P_L)
g_high

# A tibble: 2 × 8
  AUC1  LOWNEUT AUC2      n n_resp   E_Y   P_L CONTRIB
  <chr>   <int> <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 high        0 high   2400   2016  0.84  0.25    0.21
2 high        1 high   2400   1248  0.52  0.75    0.39

sum(g_high$CONTRIB)

[1] 0.6


Written out by hand, this is
\[ E[Y(\text{high}, \text{high})] =
0.84 \times 0.25 + 0.52 \times 0.75
= 0.6 \]
Repeat for the “always low” strategy:

g_low <- m_Y |>
  filter(AUC1 == "low", AUC2 == "low") |>
  left_join(p_L |> select(AUC1, LOWNEUT, P_L), by = c("AUC1", "LOWNEUT")) |>
  mutate(CONTRIB = E_Y * P_L)
g_low

# A tibble: 2 × 8
  AUC1  LOWNEUT AUC2      n n_resp   E_Y   P_L CONTRIB
  <chr>   <int> <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 low         0 low    3200   2432  0.76   0.5    0.38
2 low         1 low    6400   2816  0.44   0.5    0.22

sum(g_low$CONTRIB)

[1] 0.6


\[ E[Y(\text{low}, \text{low})] =
0.76 \times 0.5 + 0.44 \times 0.5
= 0.6 \]
The two strategies give the same mean response, so the causal effect of “always high” vs “always low” exposure is 0.


4.2.1.4 All four strategies at once
The same calculation for every strategy is one join followed by a grouped sum:

g_all <- m_Y |>
  left_join(p_L |> select(AUC1, LOWNEUT, P_L), by = c("AUC1", "LOWNEUT")) |>
  group_by(AUC1, AUC2) |>
  summarise(E_Y_strategy = sum(E_Y * P_L), .groups = "drop")
g_all

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  AUC1  AUC2  E_Y_strategy
  <chr> <chr>        <dbl>
1 high  high           0.6
2 high  low            0.6
3 low   high           0.6
4 low   low            0.6


Exposure has no effect on response under any strategy: every strategy gives a mean response of 0.6.


4.2.1.5 Why not simply adjust for \(L_2\)?
Compare this with two common analyses that do not use the g-formula.
Crude comparison. Compare response rates among subjects whose observed exposures happened to match each strategy:

crude <- subj_dat |>
  filter(AUC1 == AUC2) |>
  group_by(AUC1, AUC2) |>
  summarise(n = n(), E_Y = mean(RESP), .groups = "drop")
crude

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  AUC1  AUC2      n   E_Y
  <chr> <chr> <int> <dbl>
1 high  high   4800 0.68 
2 low   low    9600 0.547


The crude difference is 0.133. It is biased because \(L_2\) confounds the period-2 exposure: subjects with low neutrophils are more likely to receive low exposure in period 2, and they also respond less often.
Stratifying on \(L_2\). Within each level of LOWNEUT, compare response between “always high” and “always low” subjects:

strat <- m_Y |>
  filter(AUC1 == AUC2) |>
  select(LOWNEUT, AUC1, AUC2, E_Y) |>
  arrange(LOWNEUT, AUC1, AUC2)
strat

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  LOWNEUT AUC1  AUC2    E_Y
    <int> <chr> <chr> <dbl>
1       0 high  high   0.84
2       0 low   low    0.76
3       1 high  high   0.52
4       1 low   low    0.44


Within each stratum, “always high” looks better by 0.08, even though, by construction, exposure has no effect. Stratifying removes confounding of \(A_2\), but \(L_2\) is a collider on \(A_1 \rightarrow L_2 \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y\). Conditioning on it opens that path and creates a non-causal association between \(A_1\) and \(Y\). High period-1 exposure itself pushes toward low neutrophils, so among subjects with the same neutrophil status, high-exposure subjects tend to have more favorable values of \(U\), and therefore respond more often, explaining the above bias (+0.08 in “always high”).
The g-formula avoids both problems. It conditions on \(L_2\) when estimating the response means (Step 2), which handles confounding of \(A_2\). It then averages over \(L_2\) using its distribution under \(a_1\) (Step 1) rather than holding \(L_2\) fixed. As a result, the collider path stays closed for \(A_1\).



4.2.2 Example of parametric g-formula using the gfoRmula package
The calculation above is nonparametric: every conditional probability and mean was estimated as a sample proportion within a cell. The same answer can be obtained with the parametric g-formula, provided the models are saturated, i.e. they have one parameter for each combination of the covariates they condition on. A saturated logistic regression reproduces the observed cell proportions exactly, so the parametric and nonparametric plug-in estimates coincide.
The gfoRmula package (McGrath et al. 2020) implements the parametric g-formula for time-varying exposures. Its gformula() function

fits a model for each time-varying covariate and for the outcome,
simulates a large cohort forward in time under each intervention, drawing each covariate from its fitted model with exposure set by the intervention, and
averages the predicted outcome in the simulated cohort.

Step 2 replaces the exact sum over \(l\) in the g-formula with a Monte Carlo average, so the package estimate differs from the exact value by a small simulation error.

4.2.2.1 Long-format data
gformula() expects one row per subject per time point. We use two time points:

TIME = 0 holds the period-1 exposure \(A_1\).
TIME = 1 holds \(L_2\), the period-2 exposure \(A_2\) and the outcome \(Y\).

Exposure is coded as a 0/1 indicator HIGHAUC so that it can be modeled with logistic regression. There is no baseline covariate, so LOWNEUT is set to 0 at TIME = 0. This placeholder is never used in a model, because gformula() fits covariate models only to rows with TIME > 0 and takes the TIME = 0 values from the observed data. The end-of-follow-up outcome RESP is recorded only at the last time point.

library(gfoRmula)
library(data.table)


Attaching package: 'data.table'


The following object is masked from 'package:rlang':

long_dat <- bind_rows(
  subj_dat |>
    transmute(ID, TIME = 0, HIGHAUC = as.integer(AUC1 == "high"),
              LOWNEUT = 0L, RESP = NA_integer_),
  subj_dat |>
    transmute(ID, TIME = 1, HIGHAUC = as.integer(AUC2 == "high"),
              LOWNEUT, RESP)
) |>
  arrange(ID, TIME)

head(long_dat)

1     1     0       1       0    NA
2     1     1       0       1     0
3     2     0       1       0    NA
4     2     1       0       0     1
5     3     0       1       0    NA
6     3     1       0       1     1




4.2.2.2 Saturated models
The term lag1_HIGHAUC refers to the previous time point’s value of HIGHAUC, so at TIME = 1 it equals \(A_1\). The package creates it from the histories and histvars arguments. The models are:



Table 4.3: Saturated models used in the gfoRmula analysis.











Variable
Model
Free parameters
Cells




\(L_2\)
LOWNEUT ~ lag1_HIGHAUC
2
2 levels of \(A_1\)


\(A_2\)
HIGHAUC ~ lag1_HIGHAUC * LOWNEUT
4

\(Y\)
RESP ~ lag1_HIGHAUC * LOWNEUT * HIGHAUC
8

4.2.3 Example 2: Dose-mediated confounding in exposure–response
The first example used a stylized two-period table. This example applies the same ideas to a setting that is familiar to pharmacometricians: a multiple-cycle oncology trial in which exposure suppresses a safety biomarker, and the biomarker in turn drives dose interruptions. It is adapted from the dose-mediated confounding scenario in Braniff (2026). To keep the focus on g-computation, two simplifications are made relative to the paper:

Exposure is known. The paper fits a population PK model and imputes each subject’s exposure from the empirical Bayes estimates. Here we use each subject’s true exposure directly.
The code is self-contained. The data-generating process and analysis are written out below rather than sourced from the paper’s supplementary code.


4.2.3.1 Data-generating process
Subjects are randomized 1:1 to a low or a high dose \(A\) and followed for 10 dosing intervals \(t = 1, \ldots, 10\). In each interval:

Biomarker. The biomarker \(B_t\) (think of it as a neutrophil count, with median baseline value 1) starts at its baseline value \(B_0\) in interval 1. After that it moves toward an exposure-dependent setpoint with proportional noise: \[ S_t = \frac{B_0}{1 + E_{t-1}/IE_{50}}, \qquad
   B_t \sim N\!\left(\mu_t, (0.25\,\mu_t)^2\right), \qquad
   \mu_t = S_t - (S_t - B_{t-1})\, e^{-k_B}. \] Higher exposure in one interval lowers the biomarker in the next.
Dose interruption. From interval 2 onward, a low biomarker makes a dose interruption \(I_t\) more likely: \[ \text{logit}\, \Pr(I_t = 1) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_B\,(\tilde B - B_t), \] where \(\tilde B\) is the median baseline biomarker. The dose actually given is \(D_t = (1 - I_t)\, A\).
Exposure. A one-compartment IV bolus model converts the doses given so far into the average concentration \(E_t\) over the interval.
Event. The discrete-time hazard of an adverse event \(R_t\) increases with exposure and with biomarker suppression: \[ \text{logit}\, \Pr(R_t = 1 \mid R_{t-1} = 0) =
   \alpha_0 + \alpha_E\,(E_t - E_\text{ref}) + \alpha_B\,(\tilde B - B_t). \] Follow-up stops at the first event.

The DAG below unrolls the first two intervals. \(R\) stands for the event outcome over follow-up, and the exposure-dependent dose interruption is folded into the arrow \(B_2 \rightarrow E_2\).

The structure is the same treatment–confounder feedback as in Example 1, with \(B_2\) in the role of \(L_2\):

\(B_2\) is a confounder of \(E_2\) through the backdoor path \(E_2 \leftarrow B_2 \rightarrow R\) (red). Subjects whose biomarker drops are more likely to have their dose interrupted, so they have lower exposure. They also have a higher event risk because their biomarker is low.
\(B_2\) is also a mediator of \(E_1\): part of the effect of exposure on the event acts through biomarker suppression, \(E_1 \rightarrow B_2 \rightarrow R\).

So an analysis that ignores \(B_t\) is confounded, and an analysis that conditions on \(B_t\) blocks part of the effect we want to estimate.
The parameter values below are those of the paper’s dose-mediated scenario. Clearance does not depend on the biomarker in this scenario, so the biomarker affects exposure only through dose interruptions.

param <- c(
  # Dose randomization
  a.frac = 0.5, a.low = 10, a.high = 20,
  # Biomarker dynamics
  b0.lmu = 0, b0.lsd = 0.25, IE50 = 1.5, kB = 0.25, b.sd = 0.25,
  # Dose interruption
  gamma.0 = -3, gamma.B = 4,
  # PK: 1-compartment IV bolus, half-life of 1 interval, median CL of 10
  cl0.lmu = log(10), cl0.lsd = 0.2, v0.lmu = log(10 / log(2)), v0.lsd = 0.1,
  # Event hazard
  alpha.0 = -3.5, alpha.B = 3, alpha.E = 0.25
)
Nints  <- 10
B0.med <- exp(param[["b0.lmu"]])
# Reference exposure: population-average steady-state exposure, dose / CL
E.ref  <- (param[["a.frac"]] * param[["a.low"]] +
           (1 - param[["a.frac"]]) * param[["a.high"]]) / exp(param[["cl0.lmu"]])

The simulation is written as two functions. make_subjects() draws each subject’s dose and individual parameters. simulate_dgp() steps the subjects through the intervals. When E.fix is NA it simulates the natural course, the trial as it actually happens. When E.fix is a number, it simulates the counterfactual world in which every subject’s exposure is held at that value in every interval.

make_subjects <- function(N, param) {
  n.low <- round(N * param[["a.frac"]])
  tibble(
    ID = seq_len(N),
    A  = sample(c(rep(param[["a.low"]], n.low),
                  rep(param[["a.high"]], N - n.low))),
    B0 = rlnorm(N, param[["b0.lmu"]], param[["b0.lsd"]]),
    CL = rlnorm(N, param[["cl0.lmu"]], param[["cl0.lsd"]]),
    V  = rlnorm(N, param[["v0.lmu"]], param[["v0.lsd"]])
  )
}

simulate_dgp <- function(subj, param, Nints, E.fix = NA) {
  N     <- nrow(subj)
  k     <- subj$CL / subj$V
  B     <- subj$B0
  C.end <- rep(0, N)
  E     <- rep(0, N)
  out   <- vector("list", Nints)
  for (t in seq_len(Nints)) {
    if (t > 1) {
      # Biomarker moves toward an exposure-dependent setpoint
      B.set <- subj$B0 / (1 + E / param[["IE50"]])
      mu.B  <- B.set - (B.set - B) * exp(-param[["kB"]])
      B     <- pmax(rnorm(N, mu.B, param[["b.sd"]] * mu.B), 0.001)
      # Low biomarker -> dose interruption
      I <- rbinom(N, 1, plogis(param[["gamma.0"]] +
                                 param[["gamma.B"]] * (B0.med - B)))
    } else {
      I <- rep(0L, N)
    }
    D <- (1 - I) * subj$A
    # 1-compartment IV bolus: exposure = average concentration over interval
    C.start <- C.end + D / subj$V
    C.end   <- C.start * exp(-k)
    E <- if (is.na(E.fix)) C.start / k * (1 - exp(-k)) else rep(E.fix, N)
    # Event hazard
    Pr <- plogis(param[["alpha.0"]] +
                   param[["alpha.E"]] * (E - E.ref) +
                   param[["alpha.B"]] * (B0.med - B))
    out[[t]] <- tibble(ID = subj$ID, Ts = t - 1, A = subj$A, B0 = subj$B0,
                       B = B, I = I, D = D, E = E, Pr = Pr,
                       R = rbinom(N, 1, Pr))
  }
  bind_rows(out) |> arrange(ID, Ts)
}



4.2.3.2 Estimand and ground truth
We have adopted the perspective in which the mathematical estimand is the causal exposure–response curve: the risk of an event by the end of interval 10 if every subject’s exposure were held at \(e\) in every interval, \[ \Pr\left[R(\bar e) = 1\right], \qquad \bar e = (e, e, \ldots, e), \] for \(e\) between 0.5 and 2.5. Exposures of 1 and 2 are the typical steady-state exposures under the low and high dose.
Because we control the data-generating process, we can compute the true curve by simulating a large population under each static intervention. For each subject, the risk by interval 10 is \(1 - \prod_t (1 - \Pr(R_t = 1))\), and the population risk is the average over subjects.

    group_by(ID) |>
    summarise(Risk = 1 - prod(1 - Pr)) |>
    summarise(Risk = mean(Risk)) |>
    mutate(E = e)
}))

4.2.4 Naive analyses
A common approach is pooled logistic regression of the per-interval event indicator on the time-varying exposure, with a separate intercept for each interval. The fitted hazards are converted to a risk by interval 10 for each exposure level. We fit two versions, mirroring the two naive analyses in Example 1:

Adjusted for the biomarker: R ~ E + B + factor(Ts), with predictions made at the median baseline biomarker value.

    group_by(E) |>

4.2.4.1 Parametric g-formula
The g-formula for this setting extends the two-period formula of Example 1 to 10 intervals, with a continuous confounder and a survival outcome. Plug-in estimation by hand over cells is no longer possible, but the recipe is the same. We need:

A model for the time-varying confounder given the past. Here this is the biomarker model. It has the same functional form as the data-generating process, with \(k_B\) and \(IE_{50}\) estimated by generalized nonlinear least squares (nlme::gnls): \[ E[B_t \mid B_{t-1}, E_{t-1}, B_0] =
   \left(1 - e^{-k_B}\right) \frac{B_0}{1 + E_{t-1}/IE_{50}} + e^{-k_B} B_{t-1}, \] with variance proportional to the square of the mean.
A model for the outcome given the past. Here this is a pooled logistic regression for the per-interval hazard, R ~ E + B.
Monte Carlo simulation of a large cohort under each static exposure intervention. Each subject keeps their observed \(B_0\), exposure is set to \(e\), \(B_t\) is drawn from the fitted biomarker model, and the event hazard comes from the fitted outcome model.

No model is needed for exposure itself, because the intervention sets it. gformula() still requires a model statement for every covariate, so we give exposure a dummy model E ~ 1. As a consequence, the natural-course estimate in the output is not meaningful and is ignored.
The biomarker model is not one of the covariate types built into gfoRmula, so we supply custom fitting and prediction functions. The prediction function draws a new biomarker value with the fitted proportional error, mirroring the data-generating process. Its ... argument is required, because gformula() passes the intervention arguments on to custom prediction functions.

bm_fit <- function(covparams, covname, obs_data, j) {
  nlme::gnls(
    B ~ (1 - exp(-exp(lkB))) * B0 / (1 + lag1_E / exp(lIE50)) +
      exp(-exp(lkB)) * lag1_B,
    data    = obs_data,
    params  = lkB + lIE50 ~ 1,
    start   = list(lkB = log(0.25), lIE50 = log(1.5)),
    weights = nlme::varPower(value = 1, fixed = 1)
  )
}

bm_pred <- function(obs_data, newdf, fitcov, time_name, t, condition,
                    covname, ...) {
  mu <- as.numeric(predict(fitcov, newdata = newdf))
  pmax(rnorm(length(mu), mu, fitcov$sigma * abs(mu)), 0.001)
}

One static intervention is defined for each exposure level. They are built as a named list (intervention1.E, intervention2.E, …) and passed to gformula() with do.call().

The g-formula works here because the conditions from Example 1 carry over:

The confounder model and the outcome model are both correctly specified. They have the same form as the data-generating process.
Sequential exchangeability holds. The biomarker \(B_t\) captures everything that drives both the dose interruptions and the event hazard.
Positivity holds. The randomized dose and the variation in interruptions produce a range of exposures at every biomarker level.

In real data, none of these can be guaranteed. The paper examines what happens when they fail, for example when exposure must be imputed from a fitted PK model.

title: 4  G-formula and G-computation
text:
Some authors make a distinction between g-formula and g-computation, but it is a subtle distinction and it usually isn’t carefully maintained. In the material that follows, we will use the two terms interchangeably.↩︎

Our hypothetical example involves the same essential causal structure, but arising from dose changes that occur at the discretion of clinicians, rather than through stratified randomization.↩︎
The occurrence of “empty cells” is referred to in the causal inference literature as a violation of “positivity”. To properly address this topic it would be necessary to distinguish several different types of positivity violations. For present purposes we avoid these nuances simply rest with the obvious point that, depending on the available data, parametric assumptions may need to be made in order to estimate all quantities of interest.↩︎
